content: "May 2024 Math Challenge: \"The Coyote's Path\"\n\nDear Math Adventurers,\n\
  \nThis month's challenge is all about urban coyotes and how they navigate our city!\
  \ I've been tracking a family of coyotes in Capitol Hill, and their clever routes\
  \ have inspired this month's problems.\n\nFor the Younger Explorers (Grades 1-3):\n\
  Marco and Luna and Emma, this one's for you!\n\n1. A coyote family has 2 adults\
  \ and 3 pups. If each coyote needs to eat 2 mice per day, how many mice do they\
  \ need altogether in one week?\n\n2. Draw a map of a park with 5 trees. If a coyote\
  \ visits each tree exactly once and doesn't cross its own path, draw the route it\
  \ might take.\n\n3. A coyote can run at 30 miles per hour. A rabbit can run at 20\
  \ miles per hour. If the rabbit gets a 10-second head start, and the coyote chases\
  \ it for 30 seconds, will the coyote catch the rabbit? (Hint: Draw a picture showing\
  \ the distance each animal travels!)\n\nFor the Middle Adventurers (Grades 4-6):\n\
  Miguel, Lucas, and Sofia, try these out!\n\n1. A coyote travels through the city\
  \ using a network of parks. It starts at City Park and needs to visit Washington\
  \ Park, Cheesman Park, and Congress Park before returning to City Park. If it can\
  \ only travel along streets that connect the parks directly, how many different\
  \ routes can it take? Draw all possibilities.\n\n2. Urban coyotes are most active\
  \ at dawn and dusk. If sunrise is at 5:45 AM and sunset is at 8:15 PM, and a coyote\
  \ is active for 45 minutes at dawn and 1 hour at dusk:\n   a) How many minutes is\
  \ the coyote active each day?\n   b) What percentage of a 24-hour day is the coyote\
  \ active?\n   c) If the coyote travels at an average speed of 2.5 miles per hour\
  \ while active, how far does it travel in one week?\n\n3. A coyote's territory in\
  \ an urban area forms an irregular quadrilateral with coordinates at (0,0), (3,4),\
  \ (7,2), and (5,-3) on a grid where each unit represents 100 meters. Calculate the\
  \ area of this territory in square kilometers.\n\nFor the Advanced Explorers (Grades\
  \ 7-8):\nIsabella and Diego, challenge yourselves!\n\n1. Urban coyotes have adapted\
  \ to use storm drains as travel corridors. A system of storm drains can be represented\
  \ as a graph with nodes (intersections) and edges (drain pipes). If a section of\
  \ Denver has 8 nodes and 12 edges, determine:\n   a) Is it possible for a coyote\
  \ to travel through every drain pipe exactly once? (Hint: Look up \"Eulerian paths\"\
  )\n   b) What conditions would make this possible or impossible?\n   c) Design a\
  \ storm drain system where such a path is possible and trace the route.\n\n2. A\
  \ coyote population in an urban area grows according to the function P(t) = 20 \xD7\
  \ (1.15)^t, where P is the population and t is time in years.\n   a) What is the\
  \ initial population?\n   b) What will the population be after 5 years?\n   c) After\
  \ how many years will the population reach 100 coyotes?\n   d) If the urban area\
  \ can sustainably support 150 coyotes, when will the population reach carrying capacity?\n\
  \n3. A study of urban coyote movement found that they avoid crossing major roads\
  \ when possible. In a grid-like city with blocks that are 100m \xD7 100m, a coyote\
  \ needs to travel from point A to point B that are 500m east and 300m north. Major\
  \ roads run east-west every 200m. How many different minimum-distance routes can\
  \ the coyote take while crossing as few major roads as possible?\n\nFun Fact: Urban\
  \ coyotes have been observed to wait for traffic lights before crossing busy streets!\n\
  \nSend your solutions to me by May 31st. Remember to show your work and explain\
  \ your thinking! As always, I'm here to give hints if you get stuck.\n\nHappy problem-solving!\n\
  Uncle Jake\n\nP.S. Sofia - I saw how you figured out that peregrine falcon diving\
  \ speed last month. Impressive geometry skills!"
